note: The everyday hello. Any time of day, to anyone.
أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا is the full, warm welcome.
The greeting used across the Arab world, to one person or many.
Literally 'morning of goodness'.
Literally 'morning of light'.
The reply is مَسَاءُ النُّور.
Literally 'with safety'.

example.en: What is your name? (to a man)
What is your name? (to a woman)

note: مَا is used before a noun. Its initial a joins the next word: mā smuk.

example.en: What is your name? (to a man)
What is your name? (to a woman)

note: Literally 'we have been honoured'.

example.en: Where are you from? (to a man)
Hello, how are you? (to a man)

note: To a woman: كَيْفَ حَالُكِ؟ (kayfa ḥāluki).
Literally 'in goodness'.
Used by everyone, religious or not, after saying you are well.
'My father' is أَبِي (abī).
Feminine without ة: a female person.
'My brother' is أَخِي (akhī).

example.en: What is your number? (to a man)
What do you do? (to a man)

note: مَا عَمَلُكَ؟ (literally 'what is your work?') is the usual way to ask someone's job. To a woman: مَا عَمَلُكِ؟

example.en: I am a student in Cairo.

note: A female student is طَالِبَة. A school pupil is also called طَالِب.
أُسْتَاذ also means teacher, and it is the polite title for a teacher: الْأُسْتَاذ كَرِيم (Mr Karim).

example.en: My father is an employee at a company.
She is a nurse at the hospital.
Mr Karim is a translator too.

note: It ends in ى, but it is masculine: مُسْتَشْفَى كَبِير (a big hospital).
الْيَوْم (the day) also means 'today'.

example.en: There are seven days in a week.

note: Literally 'the first': the Arab week starts on Sunday.

example.en: I have a lesson on Monday.

note: From اِثْنَان (two): the second day of the week.
From ثَلَاثَة (three): the third day.
From أَرْبَعَة (four): the fourth day.

example.ar: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى بَيْتِ سَامِي يَوْمَ الْخَمِيس.
example.en: I go to Sami's house on Thursday.

note: From خَمْسَة (five): the fifth day.
The day of the gathering, when Muslims meet for the Friday prayer. In Egypt the weekend is Friday and Saturday.

example.en: On Saturday I am at home.

note: The same old word as English 'Sabbath'.

example.en: Saturday is a day off too.

note: السَّاعَة + a feminine ordinal tells the time: السَّاعَة الثَّالِثَة (three o'clock).

example.en: Do you have time? (to a man)

note: Literally 'except'. With رُبْع it takes the ending -an: إِلَّا رُبْعًا (minus a quarter).
A woman says أَنَا مُتَأَخِّرَة.

example.en: I wake up at seven o'clock.

note: Dictionaries list a verb by its past 'he' form, here اِسْتَيْقَظَ. This course shows the present 'he' form first.

example.en: I drink tea in the morning.

note: 'To' a place is إِلَى: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْبَيْت (I go home).
'From' a place is مِنْ, which becomes مِنَ before الـ: مِنَ الْبَيْت.
You know it from صَبَاحُ الْخَيْر (good morning).

example.en: I drink tea, then I go.
I go to school every day.

note: كُلَّ يَوْم = every day, كُلَّ صَبَاح = every morning.
From the same root as عَمَل (work, job).
Used for where you live: أَيْنَ تَسْكُنُ؟ (where do you live?, to a man).
For a group of men or a mixed group.
On its own لَا means 'no'. Before a present verb it means 'not'.
Short for اللُّغَة الْعَرَبِيَّة (the Arabic language). English is الْإِنْجِلِيزِيَّة.

example.en: What colour is your car? (to a man)

note: From بُنّ (coffee beans): 'coffee-coloured'.

example.en: The flag of Egypt is red, white and black.
What do you eat for breakfast? (to a man)

note: Literally 'the breaking (of the night's fast)'. 'For breakfast' is فِي الْفُطُور.

example.en: I eat bread and cheese for breakfast.

note: In Egypt the everyday round flatbread is الْخُبْز الْبَلَدِيّ, 'country bread'.

example.en: Usually I eat eggs and bread.

note: A collective noun: بَيْض is eggs in general; one egg is بَيْضَة.

example.en: I eat bread and cheese for breakfast.

note: Slow-cooked fava beans with oil, lemon and cumin: the classic Egyptian breakfast.
Egyptians call falafel طَعْمِيَّة and make it from fava beans; in the Levant falafel is made from chickpeas.
As an object: شَايًا (a tea) or الشَّايَ (the tea, tea in general).
After ة the object ending -an is two fathas with no extra alif: قَهْوَةً.
'With milk' is بِالْحَلِيب, literally 'with the milk'.
'I eat' is written آكُلُ: the hamza of أَ and the first letter أ of the root merge into آ.

example.en: The café is near the school.

note: With 'the' it is الْمَقْهَى. The word comes from قَهْوَة (coffee): a café is 'a coffee place'.

example.en: I'd like a cup of coffee, please.

note: With 'please', أُرِيدُ is the normal polite way to order: 'I'd like…'.
Ends in a hamza. As an object: مَاءً, with no extra alif.
'Lemon juice' is عَصِير لَيْمُون: juice first, then the fruit.

example.en: I'd like a tea without sugar.

note: English 'sugar' comes from this word, through Latin and French.

example.en: I'd like a cup of coffee, please.

note: 'A cup of coffee' is فِنْجَانُ قَهْوَة: the cup comes first.
For food and drink. Hot weather is حَارّ.
Literally 'from your kindness'. لَوْ سَمَحْتَ ('if you allow') is just as polite.

example.en: I'd like a bottle of water, please.

note: Also means 'glass' (the material). 'A bottle of water' is زُجَاجَةُ مَاء.
From طَعَام (food): مَـ often makes a word for a place, so a restaurant is 'a place of food'.
Any list is قَائِمَة; in a restaurant it is the menu.
A collective noun: دَجَاج is chicken (the food, or chickens in general); one hen is دَجَاجَة.
A collective noun: one fish is سَمَكَة.
In Egypt the first vowel is often dropped: ruzz.

example.en: I would like a green salad.

note: Sound feminine plural: drop ة and add ـَات.
From يَشْرَبُ (to drink). A masculine noun with a ـَات plural.

forms.label: plural after a preposition or verb

note: الْحِسَاب عَلَيَّ: 'the bill is on me'.
One verb for 'like' and 'love'. The thing you like takes الـ: أُحِبُّ الشَّايَ (I like tea).

en: I like it (lit. it pleases me)
note: The thing you like is the subject: يُعْجِبُنِي for a masculine thing, تُعْجِبُنِي for a feminine one.
In everyday speech it also means 'nice, pretty'. Sweets and desserts are الْحَلْوَى.
Hot weather and spicy food. A hot drink is سَاخِن.

example.en: The koshari is a little salty.

note: 'A fruit salad' is سَلَطَةُ فَوَاكِه.
Egypt's favourite street food, with tomato sauce and fried onions.
It comes after the verb and its object.

example.en: I don't like spicy food at all.

note: Used with a negative: لَا … أَبَدًا.

example.en: The plates are on the table.

note: Plural pattern CuCūC, like بَيْت → بُيُوت.
Plural pattern aCCāC, like قَلَم → أَقْلَام. A small coffee cup is فِنْجَان.

example.en: The spoons and forks are in the drawer.

note: Also means 'thorn'.

example.en: We don't need the knives today.

note: Usually masculine, but some speakers treat it as feminine.

example.en: We have ten loaves of bread.

note: In Egypt a round, flat loaf of country bread.
A sound feminine plural: ة → ـَات.
After a plural of things it is feminine: سَلَطَات كَثِيرَة. After people: أَصْدِقَاء كَثِيرُونَ.
The evening meal, often eaten late in Egypt.
The standard word. In Egyptian speech people usually say 'sandwitsh', from English.
A collective noun, like بَيْض: one banana is مَوْزَة.
Named after Portugal. A collective noun: one orange is بُرْتُقَالَة.
Egypt is famous for its mangoes in late summer.

forms.label: dual after a verb or preposition

note: 'My friend' is صَدِيقِي. After a verb or preposition the dual is صَدِيقَيْنِ.
The feminine of اِثْنَانِ. After a dual noun it only adds emphasis: 'two, not three'.
The feminine is عَطْشَى, without ة.
Literally 'for how much?'. Before الـ it becomes بِكَمِ.
After 3–10 use the plural (ثَلَاثَة جُنَيْهَات), after 11–99 the singular with -an (عِشْرُونَ جُنَيْهًا), after 100 the singular (مِئَةُ جُنَيْه).

example.en: I'd like a kilo of bananas.

note: 'A kilo of bananas' is كِيلُو مَوْز: the measure comes first.

example.en: What is the price of a kilo of oranges?

note: Prices in general are often الْأَسْعَار.
Its last letter is a hidden yā': غَالٍ, but الْغَالِي and غَالِيَة.
Like the sound plural: -ūna, and -īna after a verb or preposition: بِعِشْرِينَ.
From ثَلَاثَة (three) + ـُونَ.
From خَمْسَة (five) + ـُونَ.
Also written مِائَة, with a silent alif. The noun after it is singular: مِئَةُ جُنَيْه.

example.en: And here is your change: thirty pounds.
Cairo is a very big city.

note: With الـ it is also the name of Medina, the holy city in Saudi Arabia.

example.en: The bank is on Talaat Harb Street.

note: Arabic says 'in the street': فِي الشَّارِع.

example.en: First we go to Tahrir Square.

note: مَيْدَانِ التَّحْرِير (Liberation Square) is the heart of Cairo.
Cairo has so many mosques that it is called 'the city of a thousand minarets'.
From the same root as كِتَاب (book): k-t-b is the root of writing.

example.en: The tourists visit the museum every day.

note: The place follows directly, without إِلَى: يَزُورُ الْمَتْحَفَ (he visits the museum).

example.en: Take the second street on the right.

note: يَمِينًا = to the right (go right) · عَلَى الْيَمِين = on the right.

example.en: Take the second street on the left.

note: يَسَارًا = to the left (go left) · عَلَى الْيَسَار = on the left.

example.ar: هٰذَا أَوَّلُ يَوْم لِي فِي الزَّمَالِك.
example.en: This is my first day in Zamalek.

note: With الـ: الْأَوَّل (m), الْأُولَى (f). أَوَّلًا means 'first of all'.

example.en: Take the second street on the right.

note: Without الـ the masculine is ثَانٍ; with الـ it is الثَّانِي.

example.en: The bookshop is in the third building.

note: Near to = قَرِيب مِنْ. As a noun it also means 'a relative'.

example.en: Go straight ahead as far as the traffic lights.
The buses are very crowded in the morning.
We go to the tower by taxi.

note: The formal word is سَيَّارَةُ أُجْرَة (a car for hire).

example.en: I go to school by metro.
We get off at Opera station.

note: مَحَطَّةُ الْمِتْرُو = the metro station. In a phrase like this the ة is said as t: maḥaṭṭatu l-mitro.

en: to ride, to take (a bus, a taxi)

example.en: The students take the bus every morning.

note: The vehicle follows directly, with no preposition: يَرْكَبُ الْمِتْرُو (he takes the metro).

en: to get off; to go down

example.en: Where do I get off, please?

example.ar: اِجْلِسْ أَنْتَ فِي الْأَمَام بِجَانِبِ السَّائِق.
example.en: You sit in the front, next to the driver.
How much is the fare to the Cairo Tower?
I will wait for you here in front of the mosque.

note: إِلَى الْأَمَام (to the front) means 'straight ahead'.

example.en: The post office is behind the bank.
The stairs are next to the door.

note: Literally 'at the side of'.

example.en: The post office is between the café and the pharmacy.

note: Join the two places with وَ (and).

example.en: And above the door there is a blue sign.
The bag is under the chair.
The book is on the table.

note: Also in fixed phrases: عَلَى الْيَمِين (on the right).

example.en: The mosque is opposite the school.
It is an old yellow building.
The parcels office is on the second floor.
There is a pharmacy near here.

note: Its opposite is هُنَا (here).
In Egypt people address a woman pharmacist as دُكْتُورَة (doctor).

example.en: Do you have any medicine for a headache? (to a woman)

note: حَبَّة also means 'a grain' or 'one piece' of fruit.

example.en: The pharmacy is open day and night.
The first pharmacy is closed now.
On Friday I will wear my new clothes.

note: A plural of things, so its adjective is feminine singular: الْمَلَابِس الْجَدِيدَة (the new clothes).

example.en: I want a nice shirt and trousers.

note: One بَنْطَلُون is one pair of trousers: the word is singular in Arabic.
Masculine, even though women wear it: فُسْتَان جَمِيل (a beautiful dress).

example.en: The shoes are expensive in this shop.
Do you have a bigger size?
Daniel is wearing a white shirt.
The trousers are a little loose.
This shirt is a little tight.
There are many lanterns in the market.

note: Older grammar books treat سُوق as feminine; today both genders are heard.
From the verb يَبِيعُ (to sell).

example.en: This present is for my mother.

example.ar: أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَشْتَرِيَ هَدَايَا لِأَبِي وَأُمِّي.
example.en: I want to buy presents for my father and mother.

note: After أُرِيدُ أَنْ (I want to) the verb ends in -a: أَشْتَرِيَ.

example.en: The seller sells perfumes and silver.
These lanterns are old and beautiful.

note: For people, say كَبِير (old, lit. big) instead.

example.en: This necklace is made of silver.

note: The coloured lantern is the symbol of Ramadan in Egypt.

example.en: I am also buying a bottle of perfume for my mother.
Is there a discount for students?
My flat is small and lovely.

note: A furnished flat is شَقَّة مَفْرُوشَة.
Before an ending ة becomes ت: غُرْفَتِي (my room).
Literally 'the room of sleep'. 'A bedroom' is غُرْفَةُ نَوْم.

example.en: There is a big window in the living room.

note: Literally 'the room of sitting'.
Stress the first syllable: MAṬ-bakh.

example.en: And the bathroom is very small.
Is there a balcony in the flat?
There is a window in the room.

note: The opposite of كَبِير. For people it also means 'young': أُخْتِي الصَّغِيرَة (my little sister).

example.en: This is my room, and this is my bed.
On the desk there is a new lamp.

note: From the same root as صَبَاح (morning): the thing that brings light.

example.en: On the wall there is a photo of our family.
On the wall there is a photo of our family.
I have a new key for the flat.

note: عِنْدِي (I have), عِنْدَكَ (you have), عِنْدَهُ (he has), عِنْدَنَا (we have). Negative: لَيْسَ عِنْدِي.

example.en: I have a brother and a sister.

note: Written joined to the next word. Before an ending it becomes لَـ: لَكَ, لَهُ, لَهَا (but لِي, for me).

example.en: I have my phone on me.

note: مَعِي means 'with me': you have it on you right now.

example.en: This is the key to the flat.
The photos are on my phone.
We have a new fridge now.

note: From ثَلْج (ice, snow).

example.en: Do you have a cat, Layla?
What does your sister look like?

note: كَيْفَ شَكْلُهُ؟ asks what he looks like; كَيْفَ شَكْلُهَا؟ asks about a woman.

example.en: She has a very kind face.
Her hair is blond and long.

note: شَعْر is masculine, so its adjectives are masculine even for a woman's hair.
The plural عُيُون takes a feminine singular adjective: عُيُونُهَا خَضْرَاء (her eyes are green).
Singular in Arabic: one نَظَّارَة is one pair of glasses.

example.ar: أَبِي رَجُل طَوِيل، وَعِنْدَهُ لِحْيَة صَغِيرَة.
example.en: My father is a tall man, and he has a small beard.
My little sister is very pretty.

note: Used for people, places and ideas: فِكْرَة جَمِيلَة (a lovely idea).
The person you look like is the object: أَبَاهُ (his father), أُمَّهَا (her mother).

example.en: Sami is a tall, thin young man.
Omar is not tall; he is short.
Sami is a tall, thin young man.
I am not as strong as you.

example.ar: أُخْتِي هَادِئَة، لٰكِنَّ أَخِي لَيْسَ هَادِئًا أَبَدًا!
example.en: My sister is calm, but my brother is not calm at all!
Sami is a tall, thin young man.

note: The plural شَبَاب also means 'young people, youth'.
The adjective after it ends in ـًا: لَيْسَ طَوِيلًا.

example.en: Are you tall like your mother?

note: With an ending: مِثْلِي (like me), مِثْلَكَ (like you), مِثْلَهُ (like him).

example.en: My brother is ten years old.

note: 3–10 take the plural سَنَوَات; from 11 the singular سَنَةً.

en: how old are you? (to a man)
note: To a woman: كَمْ عُمْرُكِ؟ Literally 'how much is your age?'.

example.en: I'm a child, and children grow fast.
This is my uncle Mustafa, my father's brother.

note: Children also call any older man they respect عَمِّي.

example.en: Sami's aunt (his father's sister) lives in Amman.
My mother's brother is my uncle.
My aunt Huda lives in Alexandria.

note: Also a warm way to address an older woman: خَالَتِي.

example.en: Khalid is my cousin (my mother's sister's son).

note: Each cousin is named through the parent: اِبْنُ عَمِّي, اِبْنُ خَالَتِي, بِنْتُ عَمِّي, بِنْتُ خَالَتِي.

example.ar: عَمَّةُ سَامِي تَسْكُنُ فِي عَمَّان مَعَ زَوْجِهَا.
example.en: Sami's aunt lives in Amman with her husband.

note: A plural word; one relative is قَرِيب, which also means 'near'.
